section.title: The Crowning of Joshua
section.sectionRationale: The night visions end and a sign-act follows. Zechariah takes silver and gold from returned exiles, makes a crown, and sets it on the head of Joshua the high priest, then speaks of the Branch who will build the temple and rule as a priest on His throne. A priest is crowned like a king, an unheard-of union that can only be fulfilled in the coming Messiah, the priest-king.
section.thesis: God directs a crown to be set on the high priest as a living prophecy of the Branch, the Messiah who alone will unite the offices of priest and king, build the true temple, and reign in peace, so that even distant peoples will come and build with Him.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the command to make the crown and set it on Joshua the high priest; and the oracle of the Branch who builds the temple and rules as priest-king, with the crown kept as a memorial and the promise that those far off will come and build.

units.label: The crown for Joshua
units.note: a priest crowned like a king

verses.text: The word of the LORD also came to me, saying,
“Take an offering from the exiles, from Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah, who have arrived from Babylon, and go that same day to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah.
Take silver and gold, make an ornate {{atarah|crown}}, and set it on the head of the high priest, Joshua son of Jehozadak.

units.label: The oracle of the Branch
units.note: the priest-king who builds the temple

verses.text: And you are to tell him that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Here is a man whose name is the {{tsemach|Branch}}, and He will branch out from His place and build the temple of the LORD.

Yes, He will build the temple of the LORD; He will be clothed in splendor and will sit on His throne and rule. And He will be a {{kohen|priest}} on His throne, and there will be peaceful counsel between the two.’
The crown will reside in the temple of the LORD as a memorial to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and the gracious son of Zephaniah.
Even those far away will come and build the temple of the LORD, and you will know that the LORD of Hosts has sent Me to you. This will happen if you diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God.”

atarah.gloss: A crown, specifically the royal crown of a king, as distinct from the priestly turban. Made of silver and gold, it is a symbol of kingship. Setting a royal crown on the head of the high priest is a deliberate anomaly, a sign that the two offices of king and priest are destined to be joined in one person, the coming Branch.

tsemach.gloss: A sprout, shoot, or branch that grows up from a stump or root. It became a fixed messianic title, the Branch of David who springs from the fallen royal line to restore the kingdom. Zechariah uses it as a personal name for the coming one who will build the LORD's temple and reign as priest-king, echoing Isaiah and Jeremiah's promise of a righteous Branch for David.

kohen.gloss: A priest, one who mediates between God and people, offering sacrifice and intercession. In Israel the priesthood belonged to Levi and the kingship to Judah, kept strictly separate. The Branch will be a priest on His throne, uniting what the law divided, a mystery resolved only in the order of Melchizedek and fulfilled in Christ, priest and king together.

basic.context: The eight night visions are over, and God gives Zechariah a symbolic act. He takes silver and gold brought by exiles from Babylon, makes a crown, and sets it on Joshua the high priest. Then comes the word: a man called the Branch will build the LORD's temple and will rule as both king and priest, with peace between the two offices. The crown is then kept in the temple as a memorial, and God promises that even those far away will come and help build.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a prophetic sign-act with an oracle attached. Crowning a priest with a royal crown is deliberately strange, since Israel kept king and priest separate. The act points beyond Joshua to the Branch, the Messiah, who alone unites the offices. The promise of distant peoples building the temple looks past the physical temple to the wider people of God gathered from the nations.
basic.originalLanguages: The crown is an atarah, a royal crown of silver and gold, not a priestly turban, so a king's symbol rests on a priest's head. The coming one is named tsemach, the Branch, the shoot from David's fallen line, a settled title for the Messiah. He will be a kohen, a priest, yet on a throne, uniting the offices the law kept apart in one person.
basic.typology: Joshua the high priest, crowned like a king, is a walking picture of Christ. The Branch who builds the temple and reigns as priest-king is fulfilled in Jesus, who builds the true temple, His church, and holds both offices forever after the order of Melchizedek. The distant ones who come to build foreshadow the ingathering of the nations.
basic.christ: This passage is one of the clearest Old Testament portraits of the Messiah as priest-king. Jesus is the Branch, who builds not a house of stone but a living temple of His people, who is clothed in splendor and rules from His throne, and who is at the same time our great high priest, interceding for us. In Him the crown and the priesthood meet with perfect peace.
basic.god: God is the master planner of redemption, arranging even a crown of donated silver and gold to preach the coming Christ. He keeps His ancient promise of a Branch for David, unites in the Messiah what human institutions kept apart, and gathers His people from far away to build His house, all so that they will know He has sent His messenger and His Son.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 23 and 33 promise a righteous Branch for David. Isaiah 11 speaks of a shoot from the stump of Jesse. Psalm 110 and Hebrews 7 present the priest-king after the order of Melchizedek. Ephesians 2 builds the nations into God's temple.
basic.oneStory: A priest is crowned as a living prophecy of the Branch, the Messiah who will unite priesthood and kingship, build the true temple, and gather the nations. The story runs straight to Jesus, the priest on His throne, who builds His church from people near and far and reigns in the peace that the crown on Joshua's head foretold.

context.literary:
The sign-act of 6:9-15 closes the night visions without being one of them. It has no angel, no lifting of eyes, no 'What is this?' Instead the word of the LORD comes to Zechariah with direct commands: take, go, make, set, tell. The mood changes from seeing to doing, and the prophet becomes an actor in his own message. The pattern is familiar from Jeremiah and Ezekiel, where the prophet's own hands carry out the oracle, but it is rare in Zechariah, and it comes at the exact point where the visions have prepared the ground.

The passage has two movements, which the study's units already mark. Verses 9-11 give the instructions for the crown, naming the donors and the host and the recipient. Verses 12-15 give the speech to be delivered to Joshua, in a chain of statements built around the verb 'build.' The temple is built by the Branch in verse 12, built again in verse 13, and built by those far away in verse 15. Verse 14 interrupts the line with the memorial, and the whole speech turns on the repeated phrase 'He will build the temple of the LORD.' In a book written to move a community to rebuild, the verb is the point.

The oracle also looks back across the visions. In chapter 3 Joshua is cleansed and given a clean turban, and God says he will bring 'My servant, the Branch,' 3:8. In chapter 4 Zerubbabel's hands lay the foundation and will complete the temple, 4:9. Chapter 6 weaves those two strands. The Branch of 3:8 builds the temple of 4:9, and the priest who stood in filthy clothes is now the one whose head is crowned. In effect the crown joins what the visions had held side by side, and the closing phrase of verse 13, 'peaceful counsel between the two,' tells the reader how to take it.
context.historical:
The three men named in verse 10 were part of a delegation that had come from Babylon with gifts for the temple. Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah are the donors, and Josiah son of Zephaniah is the host in whose house the work is to be done. Verse 14 names the group again, with differences that the BSB footnotes record: 'Helem' appears where verse 10 has Heldai, and 'the gracious son of Zephaniah' translates a word that can be read as the name Hen, with the Syriac reading Josiah. Hen means favour or grace, and the Hebrew may be a surname or a title of honour. The variants show that the memory of these donors was kept carefully, and the crown they paid for was to stand in the temple as their memorial.

The silver and gold are to be taken from the exiles who had 'arrived from Babylon.' Many Jews had stayed in Babylon, and the returned community depended on their gifts, as Ezra 1:4 shows. The offering was therefore a sign of a community in two places standing behind one project, the diaspora and the homeland. It also echoes the way the original tabernacle and the first temple were funded by gifts from people's own possessions, and Haggai 2:8 had said, 'The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine,' about the treasures of the nations. The crown is made from the freewill gifts of a scattered people.

The most startling element was the head that received the crown. Joshua son of Jehozadak was the high priest, descended from the line of Aaron. The crown was a symbol of kingship, as when David took the crown of the king of Rabbah in 2 Samuel 12:30 or when Psalm 21:3 speaks of a crown of pure gold set on the king. In Judah's own history the royal line, the house of David, had been set aside with the exile of Jehoiachin, and Jeremiah had declared that none of his descendants would sit on David's throne, Jeremiah 22:30. Zerubbabel, who was of David's line, was governor under Persia. A Persian official might have been alarmed to see a Jewish leader crowned, and a faithful Israelite would have been equally unsettled by a priest wearing a king's crown. The text answers both concerns by making the whole act a sign about someone yet to come.
context.canonical:
The title 'Branch' stands at the centre of the oracle and has a long history. Isaiah 4:2 speaks of 'the Branch of the LORD,' beautiful and glorious. Jeremiah promises that God will raise up 'for David a righteous Branch' who 'will reign wisely as King,' Jeremiah 23:5, and repeats it in 33:15. Zechariah 3:8 has God declare, 'I am going to bring My servant, the Branch.' Isaiah 11:1 uses different words, a shoot from the stump of Jesse, but the picture is the same. A tree has been cut down to a stump, and from the stump something small and living comes up. By Zechariah's day the term has become a name: 'a man whose name is the Branch.'

The union of priest and king has a deep prehistory. Melchizedek is introduced in Genesis 14:18 as 'king of Salem and priest of God Most High.' Psalm 110:1-4 addresses a figure who sits at God's right hand and rules in the midst of his enemies, and then says, 'You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.' Under the law of Moses the two offices were kept apart, and the kings who tried to enter the temple to offer incense were struck, as Uzziah was in 2 Chronicles 26:16-21. Zechariah 6:13 is the place in the prophets where the two meet on one throne.

The New Testament sees both lines come to rest in Jesus. Hebrews 7:14 notes that he came from Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priests, and then Hebrews 7:1-3 and 8:1-2 present him as a priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek, who sits at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty. Hebrews does not quote Zechariah, but it argues the same case from Psalm 110. Ephesians 2:19-22 and 1 Peter 2:4-5 describe the temple that the Branch builds, a house of living stones, and Zechariah 6:15's promise that 'those far away' will come to build it is taken up in Ephesians 2:13-17, where the one who 'preached peace to you who were far away' makes Jew and Gentile one new man.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Zechariah's task was to prevent two mistakes. One would be to treat Joshua as a king, as if the crown made him the promised ruler, and the other would be to treat the crown as a mere gesture with no meaning for the days ahead. The oracle gives Joshua a part in the sign without handing him the office. He wears the crown, but the speech is about another, a man who will 'branch out' and build and rule. The community was to look at their high priest and see someone who points beyond himself.

The prophet also intended to widen the horizon. The temple was being built by a few thousand people with the permission of a foreign king, and it would be a modest building by comparison with Solomon's. Verse 15 says that 'those far away will come and build,' and so it enlarges the project to include people not yet part of it. At a time when the community needed encouragement, Zechariah was saying that the house they were laying stone by stone would be completed by a ruler who would also draw in the nations.

The last clause is a sober one. 'This will happen if you diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God.' The hope is certain, but the community's share in it requires faithfulness, and this clause prepares for the next chapter, where the prophet reminds them how their fathers refused to listen, Zechariah 7:11-12. Zechariah meant his hearers to leave this scene with a promise and a charge together.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The sign-act is a one-time commission to a prophet, not a rite for the community to copy. Nobody is told to crown a priest, and the passage gives no warrant for combining civil and sacred rule in a human leader. In fact the point is that it could only be done by symbol, because no human office-holder in Israel could unite the two. Churches or movements that cite this text to place one person in total spiritual and political authority are using it against its sense, which is that the union belongs to the Branch alone.

The text also contains a conditional promise in verse 15, and it is wise to be careful. The 'if you diligently obey' does not make God's plan depend on human performance; the Branch is certain. It means that those who share in the building share by listening. The principle that carries over is that God's purposes are sure, that his people are summoned to take part, and that obedience is the way a person joins what he has promised. The details of the donors and the house of Josiah are history and do not carry over as instructions.

debates.question: Is the Branch Zerubbabel, someone later, or both?

views.label: Zerubbabel, as a present hope
views.case: Zerubbabel was the Davidic governor who laid the temple's foundation, Zechariah 4:9, and Haggai called him God's signet ring, Haggai 2:23. The wording about building the temple fits him well, and some think the crown originally pointed to him and the book was later edited when he disappeared from the record.

views.label: A future Messiah
views.case: The Branch is 'a man whose name is the Branch' who 'will branch out from His place,' language that Jeremiah and Isaiah had used of the coming Davidic king. Zerubbabel is named in chapter 4 and not here, and the speech is addressed to Joshua. The wording about sitting as priest on a throne goes beyond anything Zerubbabel could be, and the Jewish and Christian traditions both read the Branch as the Messiah.

views.label: Zerubbabel as a sign of the Branch
views.case: Zerubbabel and Joshua are a sign, as 3:8 says of Joshua and his companions. Zerubbabel's work foreshadows the Branch's, and the Branch fulfills what Zerubbabel began.

debates.bearing: The third view holds what is true in the others: a historical man's work on the temple is real, and the oracle points beyond him. The wording of verse 13 can only be completed by a priest-king, which is how the New Testament reads it.

debates.question: Is it one person who is both priest and king, or are there two persons in 'the two'?

views.label: One person holds both offices
views.case: The BSB reads 'He will be a priest on His throne,' with 'peaceful counsel between the two' as the harmony of the two offices in one man. The subject throughout verses 12-13 is the Branch, who builds, is clothed in splendor, sits, rules and is priest, so the 'two' would be the offices.

views.label: Two persons in harmony
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew can be read 'And there will be a priest on His throne.' On that reading the Branch rules and a priest stands beside him, so the 'two' are king and priest as separate persons, as with Zerubbabel and Joshua in the earlier visions.

debates.bearing: The fuller New Testament reading sees the two offices in one person, Jesus. But either reading supports a harmony between throne and altar that no earlier arrangement achieved, and the text remains clear that the building and the rule belong to the Branch.

debates.question: Whom was the crown set on?

views.label: Joshua, as the text stands
views.case: The received text names Joshua son of Jehozadak, and the surprise of a king's crown on a priest's head is part of the message.

views.label: Zerubbabel, an earlier reading
views.case: Some propose that the original name was Zerubbabel and was changed after he vanished from the record, because a crown fits the Davidic governor. There is no manuscript evidence for this.

debates.bearing: The text we have names Joshua and makes good sense. The proposal, even if true, would leave the oracle pointing to the same Branch.

study.originalLanguages:
The crown is atarah, but the Hebrew form in 6:11 and again in 6:14 is plural, atarot, which some take as a composite crown of several bands or circlets and others as a plural of majesty. Atarah is the word for a royal crown, as in 2 Samuel 12:30 and Psalm 21:3. It is not the priestly headdress. In Zechariah 3:5 the clean turban set on Joshua is a different word, tsanif, a cloth wrapping, and the high priest's own headgear in the Law was a turban with a gold plate of holiness. Here, then, the priestly head is given a king's symbol. Revelation 19:12 sees Christ with 'many royal crowns on His head,' which fits a crown of several parts.

The name Branch is tsemach, from the verb tsamach, to sprout, grow or spring up. The verb is in the sentence: the Branch 'will branch out,' yitsmach, from tachtav, literally 'from under him.' The BSB renders that 'from His place,' and the sense is that he will spring up from his own ground, from beneath himself. The noun is the word of Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15, and of Isaiah 4:2, but not of Isaiah 11:1, where the shoot is a different word, though the image is the same. When the Septuagint translates tsemach in Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12 it uses anatole, 'rising,' which can mean the rising of the sun or a shoot, and Luke 1:78 uses the same Greek word when Zechariah the priest says 'the Dawn will visit us from on high.' Whether Luke plays on this link is not certain, but the double sense of rising is there in the Greek of the prophet.

The 'splendor' in which the Branch is clothed is hod, a word of royal majesty. Psalm 21:5 uses it for the king, 'You bestow on him splendor and majesty,' and it is also used of God himself. The verb for rule in verse 13 is mashal, the ordinary word for exercising dominion. The phrase 'peaceful counsel' is atsat shalom, the counsel of peace, a plan whose aim is wholeness. The word shalom is not a mere calm but a state in which everything stands rightly.

Zechariah also uses the verb banah, 'to build,' three times: the Branch will build the temple, he will build it, and those far away will build it. In 5:11 the same verb was used for the house built for Wickedness in Shinar. The two builds are set against one another across the visions. 'Far away' is rechokim, those at a distance, the term Isaiah uses in 57:19 for the nations, 'Peace, peace to those far and near,' and Paul takes it up in Ephesians 2:17.

The verb for the memorial is zikkaron, the word for something that keeps a name before God, as stones on the high priest's shoulders did in Exodus 28:12. The crown becomes a permanent reminder that the work of building was done by gifts from a scattered people. And Joshua's own name deserves a note: in Hebrew it is Yehoshua, shortened to Yeshua, and the Greek form is Iesous, 'Jesus.' The priest who is crowned in this passage bears the same name as the Branch whose coming he signals. The Septuagint's Greek of Zechariah 6:11 gives the priest's name as Iesous, which in the Greek reader's ear places 'Jesus the high priest' at the head of a crown that foretells a king.

typology.fulfillment: Joshua, the sinner cleansed in chapter 3 and now crowned, is a sign of the priest-king who is to come. In Christ the two offices stand together in a way no earthly arrangement allowed. He is the priest who 'has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek,' Hebrews 6:20, and the king to whom the Father says, 'Sit at My right hand,' Psalm 110:1. The escalation is that Joshua's crown was placed by hands and held in trust, while Christ's is a royal priesthood won by his own sacrifice, Hebrews 10:12. The type falls short because Joshua needed cleansing himself, 3:3-4, and he died, whereas Christ is sinless and lives forever. The identical name, Joshua and Jesus, is suggestive but not itself an argument.

typology.type: The Branch who builds the temple
typology.fulfillment: Zerubbabel and Joshua began the work on the house, but the Branch is its final builder. In Christ, the Branch builds a temple not of stone: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' John 2:19-21. He is the cornerstone of a house in which believers are 'being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22, and the builder greater than the house, Hebrews 3:3-6. The escalation is from a building to a body and a people. The type falls short in that Zechariah's temple was a physical structure with walls and a pedestal, and the Second Temple was in fact destroyed in AD 70, while the temple Christ builds cannot be.

typology.type: Those far away who come to build
typology.fulfillment: The distant contributors, who send gold from Babylon and are promised a share in the building, point to the Gentiles brought into God's house. Paul tells the Ephesians, 'you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ,' Ephesians 2:13, and says that Christ 'preached peace to you who were far away.' The escalation is that the far ones are no longer donors to a Jewish house but fellow citizens, 'members of God's household,' 2:19. Zechariah 8:20-23 will show many peoples coming to seek the LORD in Jerusalem. The type falls short in that the oracle names exiles from Babylon, who were Jews. The inclusion of the nations is read from the phrase 'far away,' with support from the wider prophets, and the New Testament makes it explicit.

study.christ:
This passage is among the most direct portraits of the Messiah in the Old Testament, and it reaches Christ in several ways at once. The first is by name. The Branch is the title of the coming son of David, from Isaiah 4:2 to Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15, and Zechariah has already said in 3:8 that God will bring 'My servant, the Branch.' The New Testament presents Jesus as that son of David, and the Septuagint's rendering of the title as 'rising,' anatole, fits the language of Luke 1:78. Jesus is the shoot that comes from a cut-down tree, born into a family that had lost its throne, and raised up, as Isaiah 53:2 says, 'like a tender shoot, and like a root out of dry ground.'

The second is by office. No Israelite was both priest and king, and that is the point of the strange crown. Hebrews builds an argument from the one verse of Psalm 110 that speaks of a priest forever, and shows that Jesus fulfils it: he sits at the right hand of the Majesty, ministers in the true sanctuary, and is a high priest forever, Hebrews 7:1-3 and 8:1-2. Zechariah 6:13 describes a figure who is 'clothed in splendor' and sits on a throne, and who is a priest on that throne. The Gospels give the first part, Jesus enthroned, and Hebrews the second, Jesus interceding. The union that was a symbol in the prophet's hands is a person in the New Testament.

The third is by work. The Branch 'will build the temple of the LORD.' The sentence is repeated, as if the text could not say it enough. Jesus applies the language of the temple to himself, John 2:19-21, and the apostles say that those who come to him are living stones in a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:4-5. He also fulfils the promise of 6:15 by drawing those far away: 'And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself,' John 12:32. The work that Zerubbabel began on a hill in Jerusalem is completed in a body of people drawn from every nation.

The fourth is by peace. 'Peaceful counsel between the two' can be read as the harmony of throne and altar, and in Christ that harmony is a settled fact: he reconciles God and sinners by his priestly sacrifice and rules by his kingly word, so that the one who judges is the one who bore the judgment. Ephesians 2:14 says, 'He Himself is our peace.' A people who have a king who is also their advocate before God do not need to be afraid of the throne.

Some caution is needed. It is not necessary to find Christ in every detail, such as the names of Heldai or Josiah, and the crown's physical details do not need an allegory. Joshua is a sign, and it is the Branch he signifies who counts. The passage does not mention a cross. That comes later, in Zechariah 12:10 and 13:7. Here the focus is on the glory of the one who will be crowned, and the oracle needs the other chapters to show the cost.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the planner of a long story that includes small things. He tells the prophet to collect silver and gold from named donors on a particular day, to go to a particular house, and to make a crown. The practical detail is deliberate. The God who announces the Branch also notices who gave what, and he assures the donors that they will not be forgotten, since the crown 'will reside in the temple of the LORD as a memorial.' A God who keeps a memorial for four ordinary men is a God whose attention reaches the smallest gift.

He is also a God who keeps his word across generations. The Branch was promised through Isaiah and Jeremiah, to a throne that seemed finished, and Zechariah announces that the promise still stands. The cutting down of David's tree did not cancel it. In the prophet's day the house was a pile of rubble and the royal line was a governor under Persia, and the LORD of Hosts says that a man is coming who will build. The title 'LORD of Hosts' appears twice in the oracle, 6:12 and 6:15, and the One who commands all the armies of heaven stands behind the building of a small temple.

He holds together things that human institutions kept apart. The law of Moses had good reasons for separating priest and king, so that no one held unchecked power over both worship and government. God does not abolish that wisdom. He fulfils it in one who is perfectly trustworthy, and in whom there is peaceful counsel between the offices. It shows that God's purposes may break the pattern without breaking his character.

He is also the God who gathers. Verse 15 promises that 'those far away will come and build.' The expansion of the temple project to include the distant is no afterthought but a sign of what the God of Israel intends for the nations. The same God who scattered his people among the nations will draw the nations to himself. It sets his mission outward from the beginning.

The condition of verse 15 reveals that this God asks for faithfulness without being dependent on it. 'This will happen if you diligently obey.' The promise is certain, and his people are called to share in it by listening. The tension between his sovereign certainty and the summons to obey is not resolved in the passage, and it should not be, since Scripture holds them together. In worship this means we thank him for the Branch he has sent and give ourselves to the work he has given us, with confidence that the final building belongs to him.

crossReferences.note: God promises to bring 'My servant, the Branch,' and a stone with seven eyes, and to remove the land's iniquity in a single day. Chapter 6 takes up the same Branch and shows his work as building and ruling, so the two passages are a promise and its unfolding.

Zerubbabel's hands laid the foundation and will complete the house, 'Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit.' The Branch's building in chapter 6 builds on this, and the tension between a governor who builds and a coming Branch who builds is how the prophet points past the governor.

A shoot springs up from the stump of Jesse and a Branch bears fruit from his roots. Isaiah uses different words, but the image is the same one: the family of David is cut down, and from what remains, new life comes.

God will raise up for David 'a righteous Branch' who 'will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness.' It is the prophetic promise most directly behind Zechariah's title, and it adds his name, 'The LORD Our Righteousness.'

None of Jehoiachin's descendants would prosper on David's throne. This is the problem the Branch solves: the royal line seemed to have failed, and Zechariah announces a new shoot rather than a restoration of the old crown.

The LORD tells David's Lord to sit at his right hand, and swears that he is 'a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.' The psalm is the Old Testament's other statement of a king who is also a priest, and Hebrews relies on it.

Melchizedek is 'king of Salem and priest of God Most High,' his name meaning king of righteousness and king of peace. The writer uses him to show how Jesus can be priest and king, and the peace theme matches the 'peaceful counsel' of Zechariah 6:13.

The point of the argument is that we have a high priest seated at the right hand of the throne, ministering in the true sanctuary. This is the throne and the priesthood of Zechariah 6:13 seen in the light of the cross.

David takes the golden crown from the head of the king of Rabbah and it is placed on his own head. It shows what an atarah was: a royal crown, heavy with gold and stones, which makes its appearance on a priest's head all the more startling.

Those 'once far away' are brought near, made fellow citizens, and built into a holy temple, a dwelling for God in his Spirit. Paul's picture is the New Testament fulfilment of the promise that 'those far away will come and build the temple of the LORD.'

Believers, coming to the living stone, are themselves being built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood. The one who builds the temple has made his people both the stones and the priests, which gives the vision of priest and temple a personal application.

study.oneStory:
From Eden to Sinai the Bible's story keeps an uneasy tension between kingship and priesthood. Humanity was made to rule creation and to serve in it as God's image bearers, a royal and priestly task, Genesis 1:28 and 2:15. After the fall the two functions split. Kings arrive among the nations and priests mediate in Israel, and neither alone brings God's people into rest. Melchizedek appears once, in Genesis 14, as a pointer to something not yet given, and Psalm 110 promises that a ruler will arise who holds both.

Zechariah's crown is the moment when the promise takes visible shape in a small and unlikely setting. The priest of a rebuilt temple, in a province of the Persian empire, wears a crown in a sign that the future will be different. The scene comes after centuries in which the throne had failed. It answers the exile's sharpest question, whether David's line was finished, by pointing to a Branch from the stump. And it sets the pattern for the prophets who follow, who speak of a king who comes in humility, Zechariah 9:9, and a shepherd who is struck, 13:7.

In the New Testament the promise arrives. Jesus is born into David's line and does the work of a priest, offering himself, and the Spirit he sends builds a house of living stones, Ephesians 2:21-22. The nations come, as verse 15 foretold. Revelation 1:5-6 says he 'has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father,' and Revelation 5:10 says his people 'will reign upon the earth.' The first human task of ruling and serving is given back to a redeemed people through the priest-king who restores it.

The story ends with a city that has no temple building because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The nations walk by its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it, 21:24. The Branch's work is complete: the house is built, the throne is occupied, and the counsel of peace is the life of everyone in the city. What Zechariah saw as a crown in a small room in Jerusalem becomes the centre of the new creation, and the memorial of a few generous exiles is part of a house that cannot be shaken.

quiz.q: Why is it startling that a crown is set on Joshua the high priest?

options.text: A royal crown belongs to a king, yet it is placed on a priest, uniting two offices Israel kept apart.
options.note: The union of king and priest is the whole prophetic point of the act.

options.text: Because Joshua was too young to be crowned.
options.note: The issue is the office, not his age.

options.text: Because crowns were forbidden in Israel.
options.note: Kings wore crowns; the surprise is that a priest wears one.

options.text: Because it meant nothing at all.
options.note: The act is a deliberate and meaningful sign of the coming priest-king.

quiz.q: Who is the Branch in this oracle?

options.text: The coming Messiah, the shoot from David's line who unites priesthood and kingship.
options.note: The Branch is a fixed messianic title fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: Joshua the high priest himself.
options.note: Joshua is a sign pointing to the Branch, not the Branch himself.

options.text: A literal tree in the temple courtyard.
options.note: The Branch is a person, the messianic shoot from David.

options.text: The Persian king Darius.
options.note: The Branch is the son of David, not a foreign ruler.

quiz.q: What will the Branch do according to the oracle?

options.text: Build the temple of the LORD and rule as a priest on His throne, with peace between the offices.
options.note: He builds the temple and reigns as priest-king.

options.text: Destroy the temple and abolish the priesthood.
options.note: The opposite: He builds the temple and holds the priesthood.

options.text: Only offer sacrifices, never rule.
options.note: He does both, ruling on His throne as a priest.

options.text: Nothing; the oracle makes no promises.
options.note: The oracle promises temple-building and a priestly reign.

quiz.q: How is this fulfilled in Jesus?

options.text: He is the priest-king who builds His church as God's true temple and intercedes as high priest.
options.note: Christ unites both offices after the order of Melchizedek.

options.text: He is only a king and never a priest.
options.note: He holds both offices, unlike any king of Judah.

options.text: He is only a priest and never reigns.
options.note: He reigns on His throne and serves as priest at once.

options.text: He has no connection to this prophecy.
options.note: This is one of the clearest messianic portraits of the priest-king.

quiz.q: What does the promise that those far away will come and build mean?

options.text: The nations will be gathered to help build God's true temple, His people.
options.note: It foreshadows the ingathering of the nations into God's temple.

options.text: Only exiled Jews from Babylon will ever return.
options.note: Distant peoples reach beyond returning exiles to the nations.

options.text: Foreigners are forbidden from the temple forever.
options.note: The opposite: those far off come and build.

options.text: The temple will be built by no one.
options.note: Many, near and far, will come and build.

questions: Jesus is both the King who rules you and the Priest who intercedes for you. Which of these two do you most need to lean on today, and why?
The Branch builds God's temple out of living stones from near and far. How does it change your sense of belonging to know you are being built into God's house?
God turned a gift of silver and gold into a sermon about Christ. How might God want to use your ordinary resources for His larger purposes?
The crown was laid up as a memorial pointing forward to Christ. What reminders do you keep that point your hope to Jesus rather than to yourself?
The promise depended on diligently obeying God's voice. Where is God calling you to obedient trust as part of the work He is doing?

translationNotes.note: Crown renders atarah, a royal crown of silver and gold, distinct from the priestly turban; Jehozadak is a variant of Jozadak, as in Ezra 3:2.
The Branch renders tsemach, a shoot or sprout, used as a messianic title in Isaiah 11:1, Jeremiah 23:5, and 33:15, here made a personal name for the coming one.
He will be a priest on His throne can also be rendered there will be a priest on His throne; either way the point is the union of royal and priestly office, with peaceful counsel between the two.
